title: Mothering Sunday
hook: in Britain and Ireland, mid-Lent: a day to visit the mother church and your mother

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Annunciation, a feast kept nine months before Christmas. Your line was nine months to go. What has begun in you that doesn't show yet? Day one thousand twenty-six.

A young woman walks along a country lane early on a Sunday in spring, in her one good dress, with a bunch of wildflowers she picked from the hedge. She works as a servant in a big house miles away, and this is one of the few days of the year she's let go home. She'll go to the church where she was baptized, and then to her mother's door. That's the scene tradition paints of this day in Britain and Ireland, in the middle of Lent, when the fast eased for one Sunday and people went back to where they came from. Today it's mostly cards and flowers. Underneath, there's an older idea of who your mother is. Today, Mothering Sunday.

Start with the church calendar. In the middle of Lent's long weeks, the Western church kept a Sunday with a lighter tone. Its old opening words came from Isaiah, in the King James Bible: "Rejoice ye with Jerusalem, and be glad with her, all ye that love her." A day to rejoice, in the middle of the fast. And in the English prayer book, the letter read that Sunday came from Galatians, where Paul writes: "But Jerusalem which is above is free, which is the mother of us all." Jerusalem as a mother. The church as a mother. So the first mothering, tradition says, was going back to your mother church: the church where you were baptized, or the great church of your area. People who had moved away came home for it. Then, naturally, they went home to their actual mothers too. The custom grew warm edges. Servants were given the day. Children picked flowers on the walk. Some families baked a rich fruit cake, allowed in the eased fast. Over time, the church side faded for some families and the mother side stayed, and in Britain and Ireland, Mothering Sunday became the day for cards, flowers and phone calls home. Some confuse it with the American Mother's Day. It's a different day with a different history: one grew from a Sunday in the church year, the other began separately, in America. Set the two halves of the old custom side by side: a place that made you, and a person who made you. The old answer to both was the same: a walk down the lane, flowers from the hedge, and a knock at the door.

Here's the practice: walk the road home in your mind, the way the servant walked the lane. Settle, and breathe. Start from where you are. Take the route, street by street, to a door where someone mothered you: your own mother's, or a grandmother's, an aunt's, a neighbor's, a friend's mom who fed you. Whichever door you can walk up to gladly. Notice the step, the handle, the smell when it opens. Let one kindness from that house come back, a plate set down, a coat buttoned. If you pray, you can name her before God as you stand on the step. If you don't, simply stand there with her a moment. Then pick the hour today when you'll call her, or call someone who knew her. The bell holds the time.
Mothering Sunday. A Sunday in the middle of Lent when people in Britain and Ireland went back to their mother church, and then to their mothers.
Your line: go home. Today, call your mother or a mother figure, and tell her one thing you remember from her kitchen or her door. Day one thousand twenty-six.

howItsDone: In Britain and Ireland, Mothering Sunday falls in the middle of Lent; churches often give children flowers to hand to their mothers, and families send cards, visit or share a meal.
